rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attributes in the opening oaths describe one subject, identified here as horses, and their ordered sequence follows a classical Arabic style; Ibn Zayyābah's couplet illustrates it.
rows.anchor: all of them relate to horses, and deliberation would show that there is a sequence as well in their mention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for burden includes what winds carry, such as dust and pebbles, but conventionally refers to clouds, as 7:57 shows.
rows.anchor: In general, it includes all burdens and loads which are borne by winds for example dust and pebbles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about gently moving things refers to winds, not ships; winds first blow fast with dust, then gather clouds and slow before bringing rain.
rows.anchor: The view of people who regard them to refer to ships is incorrect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Winds distribute the rain assigned to each place: some areas are drenched, partly watered, left dry, or flooded, with striking effects.
rows.anchor: these winds divide matters, which means that they rain down whatever water they had been directed to on a particular area

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The varied effects of winds and clouds bring mercy to one people and storms as punishment to another.
rows.anchor: For one nation, these merciful clouds descend as glad tidings; for another, these clouds stir up the torment of storms

rows.speaker: al-Farāhī
rows.claim: Al-Farāhī reads the promise in 51:5 broadly as everything promised by prophets; 51:6 then specifies the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: In the opinion of my mentor, Imām Ḥamīd al-Dīn al-Farāhī, the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead derives the promise from waʿīd, meaning the specific worldly punishment threatened to deniers, while 51:6 states the certain Hereafter; messengers warned of both.
rows.anchor: here it refers to that specific punishment which necessarily afflicts the addressees who deny their messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers warn of two punishments: a worldly seizure if denial continues and the Hereafter if one dies in disbelief, so both claims need substantiation.
rows.anchor: the messengers of God warned their people of two punishments: firstly, the punishment that they will face in this world if they persist in their denial

rows.speaker: al-Farāhī
rows.claim: The sky can mean the sky itself or clouds; Farāhī explains ḥubuk through knots and firm structure, then stripes and ripples in cloth, sand, water, and layered clouds.
rows.anchor: to fasten and to tie a knot.” Here it is used for the strength and firmness

rows.speaker: Imru’ al-Qays
rows.claim: The poet's description of red-striped clouds over castles supports reading ḥubuk as layered stripes and depicts winter clouds accurately.
rows.anchor: Imru’ al-Qays while praising towering castles on which clouds are overspread says

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly punishment is stated as a verb because it is a specific conditional event, while Hereafter reward and punishment are nouns because they necessarily follow from the purpose of creation.
rows.anchor: world is mentioned in verbs while the reward and punishment of the Hereafter is mentioned in nouns

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath refers to red-striped winter clouds accompanying cold northern winds, which helped destroy earlier nations; this cloud oath completes the wind oath because they are inseparable and underscores wind's destructive force.
rows.anchor: this oath is sworn by the red-striped winter clouds which appear with the cold northern winds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You are in disagreement” is a rebuke, not the oath's complement: the complement already appeared, and the second oath merely completes the first, so the verse reproaches Quraysh for irrational contradiction.
rows.anchor: this verse is not the muqsam ‘alayh (complement of oath). It is a rebuke on the attitude adopted by the adversaries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses a rebuke in place of an unstated oath complement in other passages, including Qāf and al-Burūj.
rows.anchor: A very obvious example of this has already been witnessed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contradictory claims concern the Hereafter: some disbelievers deny it, others doubt it, and many expect deities or intercessors to secure their rescue despite affirming God's attributes that entail judgment.
rows.anchor: Together with the deniers, there existed a group of hesitants who did not openly reject it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an presents an obvious reality that people would recognize if they reasoned correctly instead of obstructing their thought.
rows.anchor: is an obvious reality of this universe only if they allow their minds to think correctly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about being turned away is independent, not an adjective of “contradictory speech”; if people misuse reason and go astray, God lets their hearts stray under His established law.
rows.anchor: This is an independent sentence and not an attribute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of those immersed in heedlessness is also a sentence of scolding and rebuke.
rows.anchor: This sentence is also meant to scold and rebuke them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who reject clear signs rely on conjecture rather than intellect; speculation cannot replace truth and will ultimately prove the cause of their ruin.
rows.anchor: they are now relying entirely on conjecture and speculation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word kharrāṣūn means people who estimate; its use for estimating dates or fruit illustrates unsupported guesses made without reflection.
rows.anchor: would mean that without reflecting on something, a mere speculation about it was circulated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because human destiny matters greatly, God makes its guidance conclusive through signs in creation, sight, intellect, innate motives, prophets, and revealed books, leaving no excuse to deny it.
rows.anchor: Matters which are important and which have far-reaching consequences and on which depends the well-being and salvation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening words of 51:11 describe people who have abandoned divine light because they are engulfed by their own desires and conjectures.
rows.anchor: state an attribute of those who use their whims and conjecture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghamrah is the darkness of base desire and worldly greed; sāhūn is an additional predicate emphasizing their continuing negligence and refusal to wake from it.
rows.anchor: refers to the darkness of one’s base desires and greed for this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their question about the Day's arrival combines denial, mockery, and impatience, implying the threat is a bluff because it has not appeared.
rows.anchor: The question encompasses rejection, making fun and showing haste

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an exposes this question as an evasion: uncertainty about the date cannot undo the Hereafter supported by signs within and beyond people and by the Creator's attributes.
rows.anchor: they fully know that if the advent of the Day of Judgement is substantiated by the arguments found in the world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since only God knows when the Day will come, the Qur’an answers mockery by depicting their eventual burning rather than giving a date.
rows.anchor: instead of answering their question, the Qur’ ān has actually portrayed before them what will happen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Day they are tried, the mockers will be cooked in Fire; they may mock now, but should remember what will befall them.
rows.anchor: the Day of reward and punishment will take place when they will be cooked in Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb can mean burning or testing; both apply, and the Fire also embodies the desires and worldly adornments that made them heedless of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: This word also means to burn and heat something and also to test and try someone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes “your trial” as the worldly things that tested them and whose love made them evade the Hereafter; now those things appear in their true form for them to taste.
rows.anchor: the things of the world which became a trial for them and whose love induced them to evade the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two oaths about wind effects and striped clouds substantiate two claims: the threatened punishment is certain, and the Hereafter's reward and punishment will occur.
rows.anchor: Two things are sworn by at the beginning of the sūrah and after this two claims are stated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first claim concerns each messenger's warning that divine punishment will seize a people if they persist in denial.
rows.anchor: this refers to that punishment with which every messenger warned his people of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even powerful, resourceful nations remain within God's grasp: winds and clouds that sustain life can destroy them without elaborate means, as happened to earlier peoples and awaits the Quraysh too.
rows.anchor: God does not need to do much to ravage a nation He wants to destroy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind and cloud effects display God's power, wisdom, mercy, and providence, supplying many signs that support both punishment and the Hereafter for anyone who reflects.
rows.anchor: The majesties of God’s power, wisdom, mercy and providence which manifest as a result of the interaction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs in wind and clouds relate to monotheism, prophethood, and the Hereafter; here the author focuses on how they establish reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: These signs relate to monotheism, prophethood and the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain revives barren land through wind and clouds, an observable analogy showing that God can raise people to life after death.
rows.anchor: that very land which was once dry and desolate teems with life and becomes lush and luxuriant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The providential system of rain and harvest entails accountability: God will judge whether people show gratitude or rebel against the favors He provides, and awareness of that duty is innate unless corrupted.
rows.anchor: Will He not bring forth a day in which He judges whether man realized his obligation towards these favours

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section points to God's signs of power and providence, calls for monotheism, and reminds people that all face the same God with no other being able to rescue them.
rows.anchor: the Almighty while drawing attention to His signs of power and providence has threatened people of reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every nation treated its messenger similarly, so the Prophet should patiently continue, turn from wrongdoers, and remind those who respond; God will support him and his companions.
rows.anchor: the same attitude was adopted by every nation towards their respective messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section states that humans and jinn were created to worship God, who needs no sustenance from them and alone provides for them.
rows.anchor: I have created the jinn and men only that they worship Me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those seeking to hasten punishment should stop: it will arrive only when their appointed term ends and will be severe.
rows.anchor: those who are asking to hasten the advent of the punishment should be told to desist from this behaviour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for might can mean hand, power, or strength; its indefinite form magnifies it, while “expansive” describes God's vast dominion and ability to do the greatest tasks.
rows.anchor: also signifies power and might. It is not undefined in order to magnify its importance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's vastness demonstrates that recreating dead people is easy for its Creator; 79:27 gives the same argument, and God's power is not exhausted by creation.
rows.anchor: how can it be difficult for the God Who can bring into existence this strong and limitless sky to recreate mankind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “We are expansive” rejects the idea that God's power ran out after creating the sky; He can do whatever He wills, without fatigue from creating the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: His power is expansive and ell-embracing; He can do whatever He intends to whenever He want to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the heavens, the spread-out earth displays God's majesty and providence; its resources and nourishment show creation has purpose, and providence requires a day of accountability for human conduct.
rows.anchor: A reflection on the earth will not only reveal the greatness and majesty of God but also His providence
